en: In the root text [of the Dinakari], regarding the term *śarīriṇām* (of embodied beings), the word *śarīrin*...
With the intention of explaining the meaning exactly as it was heard, he says: "If [the definition applies] to space and the individual self (jīvātman)... Now, one might ask:

since the universals of knowledge-ness (jñānatva), desire-ness (icchātva), and effort-ness (prayatnatva) do not both reside in and exclude residence from the four categories [substance, quality, action, and generality], how can the definition be consistently applied? To this [he replies]:

He says: "hatred-ness and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), sound-ness (*śabdatva*) is included. He states the function of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*): "of the supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattvasya*). "Because of being such a quality" (*tādṛśaguṇatvāt*) means: because of being a quality possessing a genus that does not reside in what is produced and resides in what lasts for four moments. Now, [an objection]:

It has been stated that "supreme greatness" (*paramamahattvatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), but rather the state of being a dimension that does not admit of diminution. If so, how can there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by taking that [genus] as the basis? To this, he says: "In the fourth moment, of duality (*dvitva*) and so forth. Alternatively, [one might object]: "But surely, if the word 'produced' (*janya*) were not included, [the definition would apply to] supreme greatness..."

Because it exists during four moments, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time (*kāla*) and so forth by taking "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattva*) as the defining property; therefore, he says "in the fourth moment. Regarding the phrase "of duality and so forth":
"because of being such" means because they possess the quality (*guṇatva*) of having such a genus (*jāti*).
Intending the simplicity consisting in being the first to present itself, he says: "In three moments," etc. (27).

By the phrase "of the eye and so forth," the inclusion of the nose and other [senses] is intended. In that regard, even among the eye and the others, he establishes the existence of [the quality of] earthness and so forth as residing [in them] like liquidity—by the passage beginning with "ghee, lac," and so on.
(Dinakari)

He says "and it is over-extensive" because [the definition] is the object of yogic perception. For instance, in the case of the visual cognition "The pot possesses air," with respect to the air-portion—

which is a visual object consisting of presented appearance (upanītabhāna) having the pot as its qualificandum— there exists the universal *vāyutva* (airness), which is a substancehood-pervaded property residing in the air.
The term "sensory" (*laukika*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to air (*vāyu*). "Possessing gravity" (*gurutvavattva*):

gravity (*gurutva*) refers to weights such as the *raktika*, *māṣaka*, *tolaka*, and so forth. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood to include "possessing the property of falling" (*patanavattva*).
The state of falling (*patanatva*) is the state of being an action whose non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is gravity (*gurutva*).
Expressions such as "the meteor falls" (*ulkā patati*), however, are figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). In reality, however...
The property of falling, which resides in action and has gravity as its non-inherent cause, is indeed a specific universal (jāti). 28.

Now, one might object: since knowability (*jñeyatva*) is a common property (*sādharmya*) shared by all seven categories, of what could it be considered a dissimilar property (*vaidharmya*)? To address this doubt, he says: "knowability and so forth" (verse 29). Air has nine qualities, fire eleven, and water, earth, and living beings fourteen. Space and time have five, and the internal organ six.

Following the ancient verse, "In the ether and in Maheśvara there are eight, and likewise in the mind," he states the qualities of air: "In the root [text], 'the eight beginning with touch,'" meaning the eight are touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority.

The meaning is that the qualities of air (*vāyu*) are [sound, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction,] and the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called momentum (*vega*). He states the qualities of fire (*tejas*): "the eight beginning with touch. He states the qualities of water (*ap*): "the eight beginning with touch. [This concludes the section on] earth.

He states their qualities: "devoid of moisture" (snehahīnāḥ). These refer to those mentioned immediately prior. He states the qualities of the self (ātman): "the group of six beginning with intellect" (buddhyādi-ṣaṭkam), namely:
intellect (buddhi), pleasure (sukha), pain (duḥkha), desire (icchā), aversion (dveṣa), and effort (prayatna); and the pentad beginning with number (saṃkhyā).
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Because time and space share the same qualities, he refers to them with a single expression: "the pentad beginning with number.
He states the qualities of ether: "and sound. Thus, sound exists in ether.
The meaning is that number and the other four [qualities] thus constitute the six qualities.

He states the qualities of God: "number and so forth. On this point, the moderns [Navya-Naiyāyikas] maintain that there is no evidence for God possessing dimension; nor should it be argued that His possession of dimension can be inferred from His being a substance.

Because it lacks a causal necessity (*aprayojakatvāt*), and because there is no evidence for the existence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) in God; for this very reason, although conjunction and disjunction may exist there, there is likewise no evidence for them. Furthermore, the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) has already been refuted. As to how pleasure can possibly exist in God, that will be explained later.

It will become manifest. And thus they say that the qualities (guṇas) of the Lord (Īśvara) are exactly five: number, intellect, desire, effort, and pleasure. || 30 || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || Thus ends the first [chapter] in the Muktāvalīprakāśa composed by Mahādeva, son of Bālakṛṣṇa of the Bhāradvāja lineage.
Section.
Dinakari:
Since the property of being the cause of odor is present in time and so forth, he explains [the definition] with the words "gandha" (odor).

The meaning is: "possessing a genus that is pervaded by substanceness and resides in that which possesses fragrance. By this, there is no lack of extension (avyāpti) in the case of a scentless jar produced from fragrant and non-fragrant potsherds. By the term "residing" (vṛti), there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to water and the like. By the phrase "pervaded by substanceness," [the definition] excludes smell itself, which exists in those very things [water, etc.].

No; nor does it [the pervasion] hold by taking "being either water or earth" as the basis for the mention of the term *jāti* (universal), because [the property of] possessing odor and [the property of] residing [in it] are related through inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, [the reason] exists in that which possesses odor through the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), and in that which possesses water-ness (*jalatva*) and so forth through a residence delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandhāvacchinna-vṛttitva*).

There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to water and the like, because they possess the nature of water (*jalatva*), etc., which has a subsistence delimited by the temporal relation as determined by earth. [The phrase] "for the purpose of presenting a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇopanyāsāya*) is used.

Although there is no need for another means of valid cognition since the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) is perceptible, nevertheless... [Dinakari] i.e.2. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

The intention is that since perception is impossible by way of what is common to the unfit [unearthly things], it is introduced for the purpose of establishing "earthness" (pṛthivītva) by way of what is common to those [fit] things. Otherwise—
that is, if one does not accept its causality with respect to that which is delimited by "odor-ness" (gandhatva)— the consequence would be that odor is accidental (ākasmika).
The meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of [smell] not being regulated by its restricted causes.

And thus, since the property of smell (*gandhatva*), which resides in all effects, is necessarily a delimiting factor of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), it follows that earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) must necessarily be the cause for that which is delimited by it; this is the intended sense. This is also an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The establishment of the universal "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) should also be understood by way of its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*) for the destruction of color and other qualities;
[namely,] with respect to the destruction of color not produced by the destruction of its substratum,

[the cause is earthness] through the relation of inherence in the earth that is inherent in itself (*svasamavāyipṛthivīsamavetatva*), and through the relation of residing in itself (*svavṛtirūpatva*), both taken together, in connection with the relation of counter-positive-ness (*pratiyogitā*).

Because the cause is the conjunction with a specific kind of fire, and because "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) is included within the relational complex that delimits the causal capacity for such destruction; [this is stated] in the *Dinakarī*.

The qualification "unproduced" (*ajanya*) is added to the definition of destruction in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the destruction of color produced by the destruction of its substrate.

The inclusion of the term "inherence" (*samavetatva*) within the relation that delimits the causal capacity for destruction is for the purpose of precluding the undesirable consequence that the color of a cloth would be destroyed by contact with fire in a jar. Furthermore, it is included as a constituent element in order to preclude the undesirable consequence that such a color would be destroyed by means of the relation of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) in respect of a color residing in light.

The inclusion of "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) [in the definition of the cause of destruction]. To prevent the unwanted consequence that such a color (*rūpa*) would be destroyed by the taste (*rasa*), odor (*gandha*), and so forth—which are co-located with it—by means of the relation of counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*), the property of being a color (*rūpatva*) residing in itself (*svavṛti*) is included in the delimiting relation (*nāśakatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) for destruction. As for "residing in itself" (*svavṛtitva*):...
And this should be understood as a temporal qualifier (*kālikaviśeṣaṇatā*).

If the relation were "the state of being color (*rūpatva*) qualified by inherence in the earth which is inherent in itself," then, due to the lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraheṇa*), one would have to admit "the state of being inherent in that which is inherent in itself qualified by the state of being color."

The abandonment of that [position] is due to the consequence of a dual relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer. By this, [it is shown that] in the case of odor produced by heating (*pākaja-gandha*), fire-contact is the cause;
whereas in the case of non-produced odors such as fragrant scents, the fragrance residing in the constituent parts (*avayava*) acts as the regulator, by virtue of being an odor.

It has been refuted [by us] that "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) is not a universal (jāti), because there is no evidence for a causal relationship based on earth-ness itself. Now, one might raise the objection that if possessing odor (gandhavattva) were the definition of earth, it would lack pervasiveness (avyāpti) in cases such as stone, which are devoid of odor; he dispels this doubt with the words beginning with "na ca" (nor...).

"In that case too" means even in stones and the like; "by way of earth-ness" is the ellipsis. "Because of the presence of odor" means because of the inference of odor. [Objection: But if odor were present in stones and the like, there would be no non-perception of it; to this he says: "But the non-perception... [is] due to its being "not intense," that is, due to its being unmanifest. [Objection: But...

Since there is no evidence for the earth-nature (*pṛthivītva*) of stone itself, let alone for its possession of odor—which is dependent upon that [earth-nature]—he prepares the preliminary ground for establishing earth-nature in it with the words "Otherwise, how... and so forth. "Otherwise" means if earth-nature is not admitted in stones and the like; [the argument applies to] its ashes.

Regarding "in the ash of stone": although there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*) in stone— since it is simply not observed there due to the absence of earthiness (*pṛthivītva*)— and thus the effort to prove the existence of odor therein is redundant, nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated thus in accordance with the actual state of things.
Since the fragrance in stone-ash is established by direct perception, earthness must be admitted there; consequently, earthness is established in the constituent parts that originate the ash,
and therefore also in the constituent parts that originate the stone.

The nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) must be admitted [in ash], precisely because of the identity between the particles that originate the ash and the particles of the stone; thus, the intention is that the earth-nature of the stone is also established. He clarifies this with the words "for of the ash... (*bhasmano hi*). By this...
In order to prevent the non-manifestation of odor even in the ashes of that stone,
it is necessary to admit that baking occurs within the constituent parts of the stone; and thus,
the ashes are composed precisely of those stone constituents which possess the odor produced by the baking.
The objection that "the commencement [of the stone] must be from those very stones which are odorless,

otherwise there would be the inconsistency of [the scripture stating] 'in its ashes' and so forth," is refuted; for even if that were the case, the earth-nature (pṛthivītva) is established in the stone by the aforementioned method, and thus the inference of odor through that [earth-nature] is possible.

Regarding the phrase "that which is a substance": here, in Dinakari, the first word "substance" (*dravya*) is included to prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the perception of the destruction of a jar, which is neither produced from the material cause of the jar nor produced from what is not its material cause. Alternatively, it is included to prevent a deviation in the case of the destruction of color (*rūpa*) produced by the destruction of a jar. [This applies] to the "multiplication of bodies" (*kāyavyūha*) produced by the destruction of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), according to the view of the moderns (*navīna*).

The second term, "substance" (*dravya*), is included to exclude deviation in the case of a jar produced by the destruction of the prior absence of the substance that constitutes its own material cause. The term "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*) is included to exclude deviation in the case of a substance produced by the absolute absence of an obstructing substance. And here, causality is intended in the sense of being a destruction (*dhvaṃsatva*).

This is what is intended. Therefore, even according to the view of the Easterners (Prācām), there is no flaw in its being a cause by virtue of being an absence of connection with an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka-saṃsargābhāvatva*). Furthermore, "being produced from destruction" (*dhvaṃsa-janyatva*) is intended to mean "not mediated by unseen merit or demerit" (*adṛṣṭādvāraka*).
Consequently, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a hellish body produced from the destruction of a Śālagrāma stone. Not...

Furthermore, if one accepts that curd is produced by the destruction of milk and is itself produced from the parts of milk, then since curd would also possess the nature of milk (*dugdhatva*), one must admit that curd is not produced by the parts of milk; and if that were so, there would be a logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) regarding curd. This is what should be said.

Since it is not admitted that curd is produced from the destruction of milk as something distinct from the two-atomed molecule (*dvyaṇuka*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even if it is produced from the destruction of the milk-form of the *dvyaṇuka*; for curd possesses the property of being produced from the atoms that are its own material cause (*upādāna*). Nor [is there a problem] by virtue of its being produced from the atoms of milk...

It should not be argued that curd would also incur the status of being milk; for milk-ness is absent in the atoms of milk. There is no evidence for a genus that is pervaded by a sub-class of substancehood (dravyatva-vyāpya-vyāpya-jāti) to reside in atoms. Otherwise, [curd] would have to be produced from milk in the form of atoms.

Because it is impossible to prevent the occurrence of the state of being milk [in what is actually curd], and because if the states of being curd and being milk were to reside in atoms, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a confusion of universals (jāti-saṅkara). To provide an illustration for the sake of understanding the pervasion (vyāpti), he says: "And this is observed. In the root text, the possession of multiple colors is stated as another defining characteristic.

He establishes [the definition] with respect to the *lakṣya* (the subject of definition) by means of the passage beginning with "śukla" and so on. He establishes the non-existence of the application of the definition to what is not the *alakṣya* (non-subject) by means of the passage beginning with "na tu" and so on. [In the definition of substance: the term "dravyatvavyāpya" (pervaded by substanceness) is included in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to qualities (*guṇa*) and the like, which possess the universal (*jāti*) of existence (*sattā*) that resides in two forms [as both quality and substance].

The phrase "subsisting in that which possesses two forms" (*rūpadvayavadvṛtti*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to water and the like, which possess *jalatva* (water-ness) and other properties subsumed under *dravyatva* (substanceness). The term "genus" (*jāti*) is included to exclude over-extension to water and the like, which possess either *jalatva* or *pṛthivītva* (earth-ness)—both of which are subsumed under *dravyatva*. [This is necessary] because [the definition would otherwise include] the number two (*dvitva*), which consists of being an object of a specific enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Out of respect, he says: "The destruction of form" (*rūpanāśa*). Here too, the exclusion of each individual term should be understood as before. Regarding the statement in the root text that "taste there is of six kinds," he elucidates the sixfold nature of taste with the words beginning "sweet" (*madhura*) and so forth. Where there are various tastes...

[Objection: Since those [qualities] have not arisen there, there is no pervasion (avyāpti) in that case; therefore, he says: "In this case also... [Objection: But surely, by the statement in the root-text, "Smell, however, is considered to be of two kinds," the definition of earth as possessing two kinds of smell was shown, and that is incorrect because the portion concerning the "two-fold nature" is redundant; therefore, he says: "This is merely the actual state of things. In reality, smell... [End of Dinakari]
The statement "it exists in two ways" is intended to indicate this, but the meaning is that the twofold nature is not included within the definition itself.
He reveals the twofold nature of odor with the words: "And its twofold nature... (35).
He says "and thus" because the state of being neither hot nor cold would otherwise be redundant;

the meaning is that this applies even when only the possession of a touch produced by heating (*pākaja-sparśa*) is mentioned. This is because, in the Nyāya system, there is a cloth (*paṭa*) that lacks a touch produced by heating, whereas in the Vaiśeṣika system, [there is no such thing].

Anticipating the objection that the reason is unestablished (*bhāgāsiddhi*) because it exists only in atoms and not in the composite whole (*avayavin*), he refutes it with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). Regarding the phrase "produced by heating touch" (*pākajasparśa*): by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "in cloth etc.," the entire class of composites is included according to the Vaiśeṣika system. This is said with reference to the universal (*jāti*) of "existence" (*sat*).
The phrase "pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to space and so forth.
The portion "pervaded" (*vyāpya*) is included to exclude over-extension to existence (*sattā*), which is co-located with substanceness.
The phrase [ending in] "water-ness and so forth" is included to exclude over-extension to water and so forth, which is co-located with touch (*sparśa*).

Regarding the term "pākaja" (produced by heating): the word "touch" (*sparśa*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to fire, which possesses the nature of fire (*tejastva*) that co-exists with fluidity produced by heating (*pākajadravatva*). The word "universal" (*jāti*) is included to exclude over-extension to water and so forth, which possess the nature of being either water or earth (*jalapṛthivyanyataratva*). Furthermore, in this context, since "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), it serves as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

"It is not possible" means its abandonment. In reality, however, the universal "earthness" (*pṛthivītva-jāti*) is also a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of earth. Nor should it be said that, according to the view of the Teacher (Ācārya), the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) cannot be the reason (*hetu*), on the grounds that even through negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*), only positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*) is grasped; for [in this case], it is indeed the reason.

Even when there is the cognition "co-present with the probandum" (*sādhyasamānādhikaraṇa*), since the understanding "possessing the reason is possessed of the probandum" has not yet been established, there is no contradiction in [the property] being the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) even while serving as the reason; this is all the more so in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) being the means of proof. This applies even to the case of atomicity (*aṇutva*) in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

The author [Śrīdhara] says: "In the form of atoms" (paramāṇurūpa). The opponent [the Buddhist] raises an objection: "But surely... (nanu). [The Dinakarī commentary explains: "Surely the very cognition 'this is a jar' and so forth will serve as the proof for that [existence of the whole];
therefore, he says: 'By the collection of atoms alone' (paramāṇupuñjaireva)—that is, by those characterized by a specific, distinct configuration (saṃsthāna)."

The meaning is "by means of atoms alone. Regarding the phrase "from the occurrence": the meaning is "from the occurrence of cognitions such as 'this is a jar'. "Of that aggregate" refers to the aggregate of atoms.
He provides an illustration for this with the word "just as": "of that aggregate" refers to the aggregate of hairs.
"Non-occurrence" means that because atoms are manifold and minute, [the perception of "large" would not arise]; this is the sense.

Regarding the phrase "just as in the case of occurrence": just as there is the cognition "one" with respect to a collection of grain because of its unity, so too, since a particular kind of conjunction itself consists of largeness, there is the cognition "large. Thus it is.
The meaning is: "even in the case of aggregates of atoms. Regarding the phrase "because of the impossibility of being perceived":

the sense is that it is not possible for atoms, which by their very nature are incapable [of being perceived], to become capable merely through their mutual conjunction. As for hair situated at a distance, however, by its own nature...

He states that the example you cited is dissimilar because [the object] is not beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—namely, "but the hair situated at a distance" (*dūrasthakeśas tu*). Regarding the phrase "of that very [hair]" (*tasyaiva*):
"of that" refers to the hair situated at a distance. The particle *eva* (only/very) connects with the word immediately preceding the pronoun *tat*.

And thus, the meaning is that it is perceptible precisely because of its proximity. Furthermore, the point is that since distance acts as an obstacle, its imperceptibility at that time is merely conditional; it is not, however, inherent. [The phrase] "because it has arisen" [is used].

The meaning is that, according to the view of those who maintain the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the production of atoms is accepted; otherwise, if that which is invisible were to produce that which is visible, then in such a case of the production of fire, [the effect would be produced] by those falling within it— namely, those falling within the intensely heated oil— by virtue of their own nature (*svabhāva*).

Because of independence from causes. "With manifested color and so forth"—by "and so forth," light and other factors are included. "In the absence of that" means in the absence of largeness, manifested color, and so forth; the meaning is: because of the absence of largeness. Here, the followers of the Nāstika school [object]:

Although atoms that are mutually distinct are imperceptible due to the absence of magnitude (*mahattva*), there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding the perception of those same atoms when they are conjoined with one another and exist in the form of an aggregate (*puñja*). Nor is the absence of magnitude itself a sublation, for [perception] arises from that very nature of mutual conjunction which is distinct from [isolated] conjunctions.

Because largeness (*mahattva*) is the cause of visual perception. Nor should it be argued that because atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal, the perception of production and destruction in jars and the like would be untenable;
for according to that [Vaiśeṣika] system, every category of entity (*padārtha*) is indeed momentary, and thus atoms themselves possess production and destruction.

Because of its acceptance [as such]. Nor should it be argued that if "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) is admitted in a collection of atoms (paramāṇu-puñja), then the cognition "the pot from the potsherd" would be untenable, since atoms are not produced from potsherds;
for in that system, the potsherd itself is likewise of the nature of a collection of atoms.

They say: "Because they accept that the collection of atoms in the form of a jar is produced from a collection in the form of potsherds, their established doctrine is that 'from a collection [of causes], a collection [as effect] arises. That is not so; for it would involve the conceptualization of the status of being the object of such cognitions as "this is a jar" in respect to many individual atoms.

The proof of the whole as something distinct from its parts follows from [the necessity of] respect [for the evidence]; this is the general direction. In the passage "of Meru and a mustard seed," the word *api* (also/even) is connected with the subsequent phrase "the consequence of equality";
by that, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), if it were composed of parts possessing [magnitude], would itself possess magnitude.
It is accumulated. "Equality" (*sāmyam*) means the absence of any difference in magnitude;

the implication is that this is because the number of constituent parts, which serves as the cause of magnitude, is equal in both cases. And it is not the case that the parts of Mount Meru possess a magnitude equal to that of a mustard seed.

It must be stated that the mustard seed possesses a magnitude equal to its own constituent parts because of the specific magnitude of those parts; for otherwise, since the parts of Mount Meru and the parts of the mustard seed are both infinite in number, one would have to conclude that there is no difference in their respective magnitudes. Nor is this the case.

It must be said that the distinction between Mount Meru and a mustard seed arises from a specific kind of conjunction called "accumulation" (*pracaya*) residing in their constituent parts; for even this specific accumulation is governed by a specific number, and in the absence of a specific number, such a distinction would be untenable. But even so—

Since there is no evidence for the permanence of that which serves as the substratum of rest, he says: "But where... [and so on]. "Non-inherent" means the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the production of an effect that is a non-inherent positive entity. Now, even if its permanence is established, what is the proof for its atomicity? To this, Dinakara says:

He says: "By 'large dimension'... [and] "because it is a substance perceptible to the eye. Here, the word "perceptible to the eye" (cākṣuṣa) is used to exclude deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to the self (ātman). The word "substance" (dravya) is used to exclude deviation with respect to the absence of a jar (ghaṭābhāva). "Upon the establishment of its parts" means: upon the establishment of the parts of the *trasareṇu* (the triad of atoms).

"Because that is unestablished" means because the series of parts is unestablished. Here, the moderns [hold] that since the two aforementioned inferences—namely, "the parts of a *trasareṇu* have parts" and so forth—are non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), the series rests at the *truṭi* (the atom) itself. Nor...
Furthermore, since largeness (*mahattva*) is the cause for visual perception, and thus largeness is necessary in the case of a dyad (*truṭi*),

and that [largeness] is produced by the number of its parts, it cannot arise without parts; because such favorable reasoning exists, the inference establishing the dyad is not "unproven" (*aprayojakatva*).
It should be stated that this objection does not apply, because the aforementioned reasoning does not arise when one accepts the eternality of the magnitude of a *trasareṇu*.

Nor should it be argued that the existence of a substance as the substratum of that [magnitude] is necessary, since the conventional usage of the term "atom" (*aṇu*) is based on atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*).

This is because [the designation "large"] is based on a relative measure of magnitude; for even when something is large, there is the conventional usage of "larger" and "smaller. Nor should it be argued that the whole is merely a collection of *trasareṇu* atoms, because that would entail the absurd consequence that the cognition "this is a jar" and so forth would arise even when those atoms are scattered apart. Nor...

It should not be argued that in cognitions such as "the pot is a substance," the nature of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*) appears through a mediated relation consisting precisely of its conjunction [with the atoms]; for when a direct relation can serve as the object of cognition, it is more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a mediated relation as the object. This is what they say. Now, [one might ask]: by three atoms...

If it is argued: "Why does a distinct substance not arise from two atoms, as in the case of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)? Likewise, why does the production of a distinct substance not result from two dyads, as in the case of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) formed by three dyads?"—we say no. For, in the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such substances are not established; thus, [the objection fails] regarding the three atoms.
Furthermore, in the case of two dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), there is no postulation of a conjunction that initiates a substance. Here, this should be considered:

let the triad (*tryaṇuka*) be produced by three atoms alone; for there is no lack of evidence—just as the opponents maintain that it is not initiated by two dyads—for the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) to hold that it is not initiated by two atoms, since [the latter view] is supported by the force of the result.

This is because one may assume that three [atoms] simultaneously initiate a conjunction that produces a dyad. In reality, it is more appropriate for those things seen through a window-opening to be dyads, since there is parsimony (lāghava) in their being produced from two atoms. Thus, regarding the threefold nature of the body, the sense organ, and the object mentioned in the root text:

To indicate that the cause is paramount, he states the meaning: "That [body] is of the nature of an effect" (verse 37). "Born from a womb" (*yonija*) means produced by the mutual union of semen and blood. That which is different from this is "not born from a womb" (*ayonija*). "Womb-born" (*jarāyuja*) refers to that which is enveloped by the membrane of the fetus.
The term *jarāyu* (placenta) includes humans and so forth; by the phrase "and so forth," domestic animals, wild beasts, and the like are included.

By the phrase "serpents and so forth," birds and the like are included. He provides an example of those born from sweat: "worms, gadflies, and so forth. The production of their bodies arises from atoms accompanied by a specific kind of demerit (*adharma*).
The sense is: "because of acceptance. By the phrase "plants and so forth," the inclusion of the bodies of gods and others is intended;
for it is accepted that the production of those bodies arises from atoms accompanied by specific merit (dharma).

This is the state of affairs. Regarding their being born without a womb (*ayonija*), scripture itself—such as the passage stating, "Manu and others were the mind-born sons of Brahmā"—is the authoritative proof. Furthermore, in scriptural passages such as "There is no body without a womb," the word *yoni* refers merely to a cause, or the word *śarīra* refers specifically to a human body.
By the phrase "gandhādi" (smell,
etc.), the inclusion of qualities other than white color is intended; by the phrase "kledoṣmādi" (moisture, heat, etc.), [the inclusion of other qualities is intended].
Arrangement (*vyūha*) is the occupation of space (*avakāśaparigraha*). Moisture (*kleda*) means oozing (*kṣaraṇa*), that is to say, perspiration (*sveda*).

Heat (*ūṣman*) means digestion (*pāka*), that is to say, warmth (*auṣṇya*). And this [heat] is inferred from the transformation of color and other qualities in flowers and the like through contact with the body; for such [transformation] does not arise in the absence of heat. Arrangement (*vyūha*) is action (*kriyā*).

Space (avakāśa) is the absence of obstruction to the movement of food and other things within the mouth and so forth. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how is there the conventional designation of the body as being composed of the five elements? To this he says: "By that" (tena). This means:
by means of establishing the earthiness (pārthivatva) of the body. And thus, in the body...

The conventional usage of the term "composed of the five elements" (pāñcabhautika) is not based on being derived from the five gross elements as material causes (upādāna), but rather on being produced by them; thus, the distinction is that each one serves as the material cause while the other four serve as the instrumental causes. As for the phrase "but it is effort" (ceṣṭā): [the definition of] being effort (ceṣṭātva) is...
That a specific genus is manifested by effort is established by perception; nor is "bodiness" itself the genus pervaded by "earthness" and so forth, whereas "effort-ness" is—
